summary: Defines a YANG data model for key chains, lists of keys with IDs, send and accept lifetimes, and algorithms. They are used for routing protocol authentication. Overlapping lifetimes allow keys to be changed gracefully, and a data model enables automated key distribution.

plainLanguage.summary: A key chain is the list of shared secrets a router uses to prove who it is to its neighbours. Every vendor has its own way of describing that list, so a tool that wants to install a new secret has to know each vendor's own layout. This document defines one common layout, written in YANG, the language network devices use to describe their own configuration.

questions: what is a yang key chain
how does graceful key rollover work
how are key chain keys protected
subtitle: A standard YANG model for key chains, so routers can hold keys with lifetimes and swap them without breaking authentication.

tldr.problem: Network devices use lists of keys to authenticate routing protocols, but each vendor configures them differently, which makes automated key distribution and smooth key changes harder.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the ietf-key-chain YANG module: named key chains containing keys, each with a Key ID, key string, cryptographic algorithm and send and accept lifetimes that can overlap.
tldr.outcome: Other YANG modules can reference a key chain by name, and keys can be changed gracefully by overlapping lifetimes. The module is designed to be reached through NETCONF or RESTCONF.

today: RFC 8177 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata records no obsoleting or updating document, so it remains the registered YANG module for key chain configuration, with its namespace and prefix recorded in the IANA registries.

sections.title: Problem Statement
sections.content:
This document describes a YANG data model for key chains. Key chains are commonly used for routing protocol authentication and other applications requiring symmetric keys. A key chain is a list containing one or more elements containing a Key ID, key string, send and accept lifetimes, and the associated authentication or encryption algorithm. By properly overlapping the send and accept lifetimes of multiple key chain elements, key strings and algorithms may be gracefully updated. By representing them in a YANG data model, key distribution can be automated.

Key chains have been implemented and deployed by a large percentage of network equipment vendors. Providing a standard YANG model will facilitate automated key distribution and non-disruptive key rollover, and this will aid in tightening the security of the core routing infrastructure.

A key chain can be used by any service or application requiring authentication or encryption using symmetric keys. In essence, the key chain is a reusable key policy that can be referenced wherever it is required. The key chain construct has been implemented by most networking vendors and deployed in many networks.

A conceptual representation of a crypto key table is described in the crypto key table document. The crypto key table includes keys as well as their corresponding lifetimes and algorithms, and additionally includes key selection criteria, designed for a deployment model where the details of the applications requiring authentication or encryption permeate into the key database. The YANG key chain model described here does not include key selection criteria or support that deployment model, though it does not preclude it; another document describes augmentations to the key chain YANG model in support of key selection criteria.

In some applications the protocols do not use the key chain element key directly, but a key derivation function is used to derive a short-lived key from it.
sections.plainLanguage: The idea is to make the key list a named object that anything can point at. A routing protocol says which key chain to use for a neighbour, and the key chain itself holds the keys, their lifetimes and their algorithms. Because the model is the same everywhere, a management system can distribute a new secret to a whole site without knowing which vendor built each router.

sections.title: Graceful Key Rollover Using Key Chains
sections.content:
Key chains may be used to gracefully update the key string and/or algorithm used by an application for authentication or encryption. To achieve graceful key rollover, the receiver MAY accept all the keys that have a valid accept lifetime, and the sender MAY send the key with the most recent send lifetime.

The document gives a scenario for facilitating key rollover. First, distribute a key chain with a new key to all the routers or other network devices in the domain of that key chain; the new key's accept lifetime should be such that it is accepted during the key rollover period, and the send lifetime should be a time in the future when it can be assured that all the routers in the domain of that key are upgraded, which has no immediate impact on the keys used for transmission. Second, assure that all the network devices have been updated with the updated key chain and that their system times are roughly synchronized. The system times of devices within an administrative domain are commonly synchronized, for example using the Network Time Protocol, and this step may also be automated. Third, when the send lifetime of the new key becomes valid, the network devices within the domain will use the new key for transmissions. Fourth, at some point in the future a new key chain with the old key removed may be distributed to the devices, and this may be deferred until the next key rollover. If this is done, the key chain will always include two keys: either the current and future key during key rollovers, or the current and previous keys between key rollovers.

Since the most recent send lifetime is defined as the one with the latest start-time, specification of always will prevent using the graceful key rollover technique. Other key configuration and usage scenarios are possible, but they are beyond the scope of this document.
sections.plainLanguage: The trick is to overlap two keys. Every device is given the new key with an accept lifetime that starts now but a send lifetime that starts later. Until that moment everyone keeps using the old key, so nothing breaks. When the moment arrives, everyone switches to the new one, because they all had it already. The old key is removed at the next rollover. The clocks have to be roughly in step, which is why the document mentions time synchronisation.

sections.title: Design of the Key Chain Model
sections.content:
The ietf-key-chain module contains a list of one or more keys indexed by a Key ID. For some applications, such as OSPFv3, the Key ID is used to identify the key chain key to be used. In addition to the Key ID, each key chain key includes a key string and a cryptographic algorithm. Optionally, the key chain keys include send and accept lifetimes. If the send or accept lifetime is unspecified, the key is always considered valid.

Different key values for transmission versus acceptance may be supported with multiple key chain elements. The key used for transmission will have a valid send-lifetime and invalid accept-lifetime, for example an end-time equal to the start-time, and the key used for acceptance will have a valid accept-lifetime and invalid send-lifetime. Due to the differences in key chain implementations across various vendors, some of the data elements are optional. The crypto algorithm identities are provided for reuse when configuring legacy authentication and encryption not using key chains.

A key chain is identified by a unique name within the scope of the network device, and the key-chain-ref typedef SHOULD be used by other YANG modules when they need to reference a configured key chain. Other YANG modules may reference the key chain names for authentication and encryption applications, and a YANG type has been provided to facilitate reference to the key-chain name without having to specify the complete YANG XML Path Language expression.

The key chain operational state is included in the same tree as key chain configuration, consistent with the Network Management Datastore Architecture. The timestamp of the last key chain modification is also maintained in the operational state, and the operational state includes an indication of whether or not a key chain key is valid for transmission or acceptance.

Features are used to handle differences between vendor implementations. For example, not all vendors support configuration of an acceptance tolerance or configuration of key strings in hexadecimal. Features are also used to support security requirements not yet implemented by vendors or implemented by only a single vendor. It is common for an entity with sufficient permissions to read and store a device's configuration, which would include the contents of this model, so to avoid unnecessarily seeing and storing the keys in cleartext the model provides an aes-key-wrap feature.
sections.plainLanguage: Each key has a number that identifies it, the secret itself, the algorithm to use with it, and optionally a window during which it is valid for sending and a window during which it is valid for receiving. A key chain is just a name for a list of these. The model also reports back which keys are currently valid for sending and which for receiving, and how long it has been since anybody changed the chain.

sections.title: The Model Tree
sections.content:
The model tree has a container of key chains, each identified by its name. A key chain holds a name, an optional description, an optional accept-tolerance container holding a duration in seconds, and a read-only last-modified timestamp. Inside it is a list of keys, each keyed by its key-id. A key holds the key-id, a lifetime container, a mandatory crypto-algorithm, a key-string container and two read-only booleans saying whether the send lifetime and the accept lifetime are currently active. Separately, the tree has an aes-key-wrap container with an enable flag.

The lifetime container offers a choice between a single send-and-accept lifetime, which uses the shared lifetime grouping, and independent send and accept lifetimes, which is behind the independent-send-accept-lifetime feature. The lifetime grouping itself is a choice with a default of always, and otherwise a start-date-time together with an end-time choice offering infinite, a duration in seconds, or an end date and time. The duration has a range of 1 to 2147483646 seconds. The key-string container offers either an ASCII keystring or a hexadecimal string behind the hex-key-string feature, and the hexadecimal form affords greater key entropy with the same number of internal key-string octets, and discourages the use of well-known words or numbers. The key strings are not accessible by default and access control rules are required to configure or retrieve them.
sections.plainLanguage: The tree is the shape of the configuration: a list of key chains, each a list of keys, each with its lifetimes and its secret. A lifetime can be always, or it can start at a given moment and end at a given moment, after a number of seconds, or never. The secret can be written as text or as hexadecimal, and hexadecimal is preferred because it packs more randomness into the same space and stops people picking memorable words.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The YANG module defined in this document is designed to be accessed via network management protocols such as NETCONF or RESTCONF. The lowest NETCONF layer is the secure transport layer, and the mandatory-to-implement secure transport is Secure Shell. The lowest RESTCONF layer is HTTPS, and the mandatory-to-implement secure transport is TLS.

The NETCONF access control model provides the means to restrict access for particular users to a pre-configured subset of all available protocol operations and content. The key strings are not accessible by default, and access control model rules are required to configure or retrieve them.

When configured, the key strings can be encrypted using the AES Key Wrap algorithm. The AES key-encryption key is not included in the YANG model and must be set or derived independently of key chain configuration. When AES key encryption is used, the hex-key-string feature is also required, since the encrypted keys will contain characters that are not representable in the YANG string built-in type. It is RECOMMENDED that key strings be encrypted using AES key encryption to prevent key chains from being retrieved and stored with the key strings in cleartext, and this recommendation is independent of the access protection available from the access control model.

The cleartext algorithm is included as a YANG feature. Its usage is NOT RECOMMENDED except in cases where the application and device have no other alternative, such as a legacy network device that must authenticate packets at intervals of 10 milliseconds or less for many peers using Bidirectional Forwarding Detection. Keys used with the cleartext algorithm are considered insecure and SHOULD NOT be reused with more secure algorithms. Similarly, the MD5 and SHA-1 algorithms have been proven to be insecure, and their usage is NOT RECOMMENDED; usage should be confined to deployments where it is required for backward compatibility. Implementations with keys provided via this model should store them using best current security practices.
sections.plainLanguage: Two layers of protection. The management session itself is protected, by SSH for NETCONF and TLS for RESTCONF, and access control rules keep ordinary users away from the secrets. On top of that, the secrets can be stored wrapped with AES so that a backup of the configuration does not contain them in the clear. The document is blunt about the old algorithms: cleartext, MD5 and SHA-1 are all not recommended.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
This document registers a URI in the IETF XML Registry, with the IESG as the registrant contact. The URI is urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-key-chain, and the requested URI is an XML namespace.

This document also registers a YANG module in the YANG Module Names registry: the name is ietf-key-chain, the namespace is urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-key-chain, the prefix is key-chain, and the reference is RFC 8177.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA records the module name, its namespace and its prefix, so that other modules and tools can refer to it unambiguously.

viz.caption: The four steps of a graceful key rollover

items.title: 1. Distribute the new key
items.text: Send the new key to every device, with an accept lifetime that starts now and a send lifetime that starts once every device is known to have it.

items.title: 2. Check the clocks
items.text: Make sure the system times of the devices are roughly synchronized, so that every device switches at the same moment.

items.title: 3. Switch on the send lifetime
items.text: When the send lifetime becomes valid, the devices start using the new key for transmissions.

items.title: 4. Remove the old key later
items.text: A key chain with the old key removed can be distributed at the next rollover, so the chain always holds the current and previous, or current and future, key.
